https://www.dw.com/en/homemade-bomb-goes.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I8hK Armed law enforcement officers have closed off the area to the public Image: Belkin Alexey/Russian Look/IMAGO Advertisement An explosion at a restaurant in central Moscow killed at least three people, including the suspected bomber on Saturday night, authorities said. Russia's Anti-Terrorism Committee said a woman carrying "a homemade explosive device" tried to enter the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square but was stopped by a security guard. The device exploded at the entrance, killing the woman, the guard and a restaurant patron. What do we know about the explosion? State news agency RIA Novosti reported that at least 21 other people were injured in the blast, which occurred shortly before 8 p.m. local time (5 p.m. UTC). The restaurant's website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a private event. The explosion occurred at an Italian restaurant located in one of ​Moscow's seven Stalin-era skyscrapers Image: Sergei Vedyashkin/Moscow News Agency/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Heavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the area and launched an investigation. Authorities did not immediately identify those they believed to be behind the attack. Russia has faced several attacks since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. They blamed a ‌series of assassinations and attempted killings on Kyiv. https://www.dw.com/en/white-house-bars-c.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NK2D Trump banned reporters from CNN from White House grounds earlier this week, with main networks having suspended coverage in solidarity as well Image: Bonnie Cash/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance Advertisement American news broadcaster CNN said its journalists were not allowed to board Air Force One for a planned trip with President Donald Trump on Saturday. CNN was scheduled to travel on Air Force One to Knoxville, Tennessee, where Trump was expected to watch a college football game. The news organization was to be the representative of the TV press pool for the weekend, meaning that it would cover the president and share video and information with the four other big networks that are part of the press pool. CNN was replaced by Real America's Voice News, a conservative network, the Associated Press reported. The episode represents the latest showdown between the Trump administration and media networks that the president believes to be unfavorable in their coverage. Trump bans media outlets from White House To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Trump bans CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from White House Trump earlier this week barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House after he said the networks report "fiction and lies." Major TV networks, including DW , then cut off their pooled coverage of the president in solidarity. A federal judge temporarily struck down the ban in a ruling on Thursday after the outlets filed a lawsuit. But the order from the judge addressed "hard passes" to the White House grounds and didn't directly address pool duties. https://www.politico.eu/article/corrupti.text: The European Commission’s bid to make the EU’s billions more responsive to the unknown crises of the future might also make them more prone to misuse, the EU’s top spending watchdog warned. European Court of Auditors President Tony Murphy said key pillars of the Commission’s plan to overhaul the EU’s long-term budget would muddy the view for those in charge of making sure public money is spent as intended. “It’s more difficult for us to follow the money,” Murphy said. “You’re saying to the member state, here’s a whole lot of money, and you make sure everything is okay. It’s sort of a self-policing.” Advertisement Advertisement The warning comes as EU leaders continue fighting over the price tag for the EU’s post-2027 budget in Brussels this week — and as the auditors document an increase in misspending of taxpayer funds. Yet separate from the budget’s bottom line is the debate over how that money gets divided. As a spending cycle marked by the pandemic, wars and climate-fueled disruption comes to a close, the Commission wants to make the next seven-year budget more agile by assigning about half of it — almost a trillion euros over seven years — to a single pot of money that countries can spend on objectives ranging from migration to agriculture and regional development. Those agriculture and regional development funds — often delivered in the form of subsidies to farms and local projects — have long been vulnerable to fraud and misuse. According to Murphy, giving capitals more leeway to shift spending would make spending even harder to track. “There will be some flexibility, but at what cost?” he said in an interview. More of the oversight will depend on the checks each country has already put in place. As it stands, misspending of the EU budget was on the rise last year, with errors affecting transactions for an estimated €5 billion according to the ECA’s latest report. Advertisement Advertisement In the next EU budget, it might not be possible to even estimate such a number, Murphy warned, as each country’s auditors have different roles and ways of doing things. His head of cabinet, Wolfgang Stolz, added during the interview: “Year after year we have found that the work of these auditing authorities is not fully reliable.” In a statement, the Commission defended its proposal, underlining that “key principles” of the current control system will remain in place. National authorities are “well-functioning,” the statement contended, but added that the Commission would maintain the right to ask capitals to “amend the plan or introduce correction mechanisms if needed.” ‘Mixed bag’ One of the Commission’s proposed innovations is putting the Common Agricultural Policy — historically a standalone budget line — into a behemoth umbrella fund known as the National and Regional Partnership Plans. Murphy stressed that he’s not advocating for any model over the other. But as EU money increasingly merges with national budgets, it will be harder for Brussels to monitor where its money actually goes. The CAP is simpler to audit when “it’s not mixed up in this mixed bag,” Murphy said. Headlines about farm subsidies paying for fake pastures in Greece and cash meant to support rural tourism in Slovakia instead going to luxury villas for the rich offer lurid illustrations of the challenge of policing these funds under the current system. And the model for the new spending system — the EU’s post-Covid recovery fund — doesn’t bode well, Murphy said. While it became easier for countries to direct the funds where they were needed, the spending also became more opaque. The new national plans were designed using the same blueprint. Under the current budget system, the ECA can physically visit a farm that receives EU funds. However, under the Covid recovery fund, the EU publishes only the top 100 beneficiaries each year. “It’s not very transparent. I mean, where is the EU money actually ending up? That’s what matters,” Murphy said. “You have a fund where there are different policy areas with completely different objectives and timeframes, different delivery mechanisms and less predictability.” Advertisement Advertisement
